coverage.category: 1. Household employers: domestic workers, live-in carers, nannies
coverage.found: Nothing new beyond K15 (SIPE free for domestic employers). Not searched again.

coverage.category: 2. Scrap-metal dealers
coverage.found: Nothing new beyond K04. My search for 'Ley 542' returned no Panama hit, so the law number and the MICI scrap register are unverified from my side. INTELCOM (MICI) report notes many urban scrap collectors and ferrous scrap as a top export; MEF auctions state scrap to Panascrap, Panama Metal Recycling and Imperial Recycling.

coverage.category: 3. Second-hand dealers and pawnbrokers
coverage.found: Pawnshops (about 190 MICI-authorised, older figure) and precious-metal dealers are AML 'sujetos obligados no financieros' under Ley 23/2015, supervised by the Superintendencia de Sujetos No Financieros (Ley 124/2020). SSNF signed a cooperation deal with the Asociación de Entidades Prendarias de Panamá. Res. S-008-2026 (Mar 2026) tightens PEP due diligence. Licence side is K16; AML side is a new candidate (C1).

coverage.category: 4. Gold and jewellery buyers
coverage.found: Jewellers and precious metals/stones traders are covered by the same SSNF AML regime and S-008-2026 (see C1). No 'compro oro' specific notice-of-operation deadline found.

coverage.category: 5. Used car parts and vehicle dismantlers
coverage.found: Nothing found: no Panama dismantler/desguace register or 2025 law surfaced. ATTT is only tightening inspection (revisado) workshops. Looks like a regulatory gap rather than a duty.

coverage.category: 6. Livestock traders, markets and animal transport
coverage.found: Nothing new beyond K05. Bovine traceability rolled out from Chiriquí 2015, national target 2019; movement restrictions apply to herds without traceability registration (Barú, Renacimiento). Current status of the national system unverified.

coverage.category: 7. Small abattoirs and butchers
coverage.found: MINSA follow-ups on butchers selling meat of doubtful origin (Jul 2026), INEC slaughter statistics; no new recurring filing found. Nothing new beyond K05.

coverage.category: 8. Beekeepers
coverage.found: About 400 registered beekeepers and 8,653 hives (MIDA survey 2019); MINSA sanitary-registration sweeps on honey. No recurring filing, tiny buyer group (C10 weak).

coverage.category: 9. Veterinary practices and veterinary medicine sellers
coverage.found: MIDA 'oficinas registrantes' of veterinary products need a regente veterinario and an inspection (B/.100). Panama adopted RTCA 65.05.51:08 by DE 99/2015; whether the 2018 revision (RTCA 65.05.51:18) is adopted is unverified. No recurring register for clinics found (C9 weak).

coverage.category: 10. Well drillers and water abstraction
coverage.found: MiAmbiente study found over 4,000 wells, only about 1,300 with permits/concessions; drillers must be in the Registro de Perforadores de Subsuelo (Res. DM-0476-2019). Enforcement push, mainly Azuero dry arc. Candidate C6. The MiAmbiente PDF could not be read, so regularisation deadlines are unverified.

coverage.category: 11. Septic, sanitation and waste haulers
coverage.found: Nothing found on a septic-hauler register or waste manifest for small haulers. MiAmbiente fines focus on treatment plants and discharge permits. Unverified; may exist under the waste law.

coverage.category: 12. Lift, boiler and pressure-equipment owners and inspectors
coverage.found: No national lift/boiler inspection law found. Bomberos urge monthly lift maintenance (2026) and fire-pump servicing must be done by firms registered in JTIA and the Bomberos fire directorate (Res. 102-2023). Fire side is K11. Nothing new.

coverage.category: 13. Small water systems
coverage.found: JAAR (rural water boards, under 1,500 inhabitants) governed by DE 1839/2014, supported by MINSA DISAPAS; BID says quality monitoring is sporadic. No reporting format found (C7 weak: non-profit community buyers).

coverage.category: 14. Pesticide and fertiliser dealers and applicators
coverage.found: Ley 47/1996 and DE 63/1997 (MIDA Sanidad Vegetal). Res. OAL-051-ADM-2025 (published 25 Apr 2025) bans/cancels WHO 1a/1b toxicology products; a separate MIDA resolution banned eight highly hazardous pesticides with an 18-month sell-down period. Candidate C3 (one-off deadline). The Gaceta PDF could not be read.

coverage.category: 15. Labour contractors and recruitment agencies
coverage.found: Private placement agencies need a Mitradel licence (DE 32/2016), about 75 agencies, must file periodic reports and register outsourcing contracts (max 2 months). Candidate C5; small buyer pool.

coverage.category: 16. Cemeteries, burial societies and funeral services
coverage.found: No licensing or reporting regime for private cemeteries or funeral homes found. Only the one-off DE 26 of 21 Jul 2026 closing eight cemeteries for the Río Indio reservoir (last burials 15 Jan 2027). Not a software case.

coverage.category: 17. Community and religious bodies: associations, charities, halal and kosher supervision
coverage.found: Associations and foundations are supervised by Ministerio de Gobierno; DE 168/2024 sets accounting-records duty; MEF suspended the tax benefit of a group of NGOs in Jun 2025 after a DGI review; MIDES audits NGOs that receive subsidies (Mar 2025). Candidate C4. Halal/kosher: nothing found.

coverage.category: 18. Transport operators: minibus, taxi, moto-taxi, small trucking and bus fleets
coverage.found: ATTT started mandatory technical verification for 2026 plates in Sep 2026 for taxis, collective buses, school transport and tourism service (K17 covers taxis). New certificates for taxis in Panamá and San Miguelito were frozen in an older note. Candidate C8 for non-taxi fleets (weak). Trucking and moto-taxi: nothing found.

coverage.category: 19. Market traders, street vendors, money changers
coverage.found: Budget used on other categories; no search run. Money-changer AML falls under the banking superintendency and is outside this niche.

coverage.category: 20. Small licensed premises with inspections: tattoo studios, driving schools, childminders and nurseries, small food producers, hunting outfitters
coverage.found: Driving schools: Resuelto 380 of 2000; ATTT reactivated authorisation after two decades and authorised 34 schools in Dec 2025 (about 100 existed earlier); renewal call ran 16 Aug-29 Nov 2024; instructors must be certified (Udelas/Inadeh); fines B/.50-500 (C2). Private childcare (CAIPI) about 220 centres supervised by MIDES under DE 107/2017, operating notice via MICI (C9b). Tattoo studios, hunting outfitters and small food producers: not searched.

coverage.category: 24. Private clinics, labs and other health providers that bill insurers or state schemes
coverage.found: No Panamanian mandate for private clinics or labs on electronic clinical records or CSS registration found. Only Decreto Ejecutivo 25/2022 on e-invoicing (covered by K06/K12) and an IDB MINSA-CSS integration project (public sector). A MINSA-CSS deal with clinical lab technicians (31 Jul 2026) was not readable. Nothing new.

coverage.category: 25. Pharmacies, medicine importers, and users of controlled chemicals or precursors
coverage.found: DNFD Comunicado 021-2024: every pharmacy must send a quarterly controlled-substances report (scanned PDF of the paper form, purchases and returns detail) by e-mail with the licence number in the subject. DNFD ran 888 inspections Jan-May 2026, and about 59% of May activity was checking controlled-substance inventories. Ley 419 of 1 Feb 2024 is the new DNFD framework. Comunicado 019-DNFD-2026 requires a licence modification for pharmacies that will sell medicinal cannabis derivatives (Ley 242/2021, DE 6/2025). No medicine serialisation rule found. Chemical-precursor users not searched. Two candidates listed.

coverage.category: 26. Security, cleaning and manpower agencies, and the firms that hire their workers
coverage.found: MINSEG/DIASP authorises private security agencies (DE 21 and 22 of 1992; Ley 57/2011 for arms); more than 357 registered. Mitradel inspections found illegal arms and foreign staff without permits; unions allege unpaid CSS dues. Forms ASEG-PORTE/2025 and ASEG-ARMAS/2025 exist. No periodic payroll or staff-register filing found. Cleaning and manpower agencies not searched. Weak candidate only.

coverage.category: 27. Construction, mining and quarry contractors and suppliers: site registers, accreditation, local-content reports
coverage.found: No new contractor register found. Public procurement Ley 153/2020 and DE 40/2018 (beneficial-ownership declaration for bidders). Quarries: about 154 non-metallic concessions (MICI Recursos Minerales, Nov 2022); Arraiján municipality moved quarry tax to extracted volume and recovered about $100k of unreported material. No MICI periodic report found. Ley 518 (Apr 2026) on recycled tyres in asphalt is for road works, not a duty on small firms.

coverage.category: 28. Notaries, land agents, real estate brokers and other professionals with periodic or anti-money-laundering reports
coverage.found: SSNF (Ley 124/2020) supervises about 12,000 non-financial obliged subjects plus about 7,500 resident agents; more than 60% are lawyers. Resolution S-022-2025 (21 Mar 2025, Gaceta 1 Apr 2025) imposes risk self-assessment questionnaires. Registration on the SSNF online app (Res. S-010-2021), fine $5,000 for not registering. UAF secure platform needs an ADSO code for STR/cash reports. Beneficial-owner register (RUBF) 91% loaded. MIVIOT is reviewing the real-estate law (Junta Tecnica de Bienes Raices; watch). Real-estate brokers are already K03; resident agents K01. A broader professional buyer is listed as a new candidate.

coverage.category: 29. Hotels, guest houses and short-term rentals: guest registers, tourism levies
coverage.found: Ley 80/2012 (art. 21) bans stays under 45 days in Panama district without ATP permit; not enforced. July 2025 proposals (ATP general tourism law, deputy Zamora bill) would require ATP registration, invoices and ITBMS for platform hosts. No enacted 2026 rule found. ATP counts 2,798 hostels registered (2025). Fines $5,000-$50,000 for clandestine lodging. No guest-register mandate to Migracion found (consistent with K10). Watch item only.

coverage.category: 30. Small exporters and importers facing traceability or certification rules: food, fish, timber, forest-risk commodities
coverage.found: Fisheries: Ley 204/2021 and its 2024 regulation. A national traceability system was due July 2026 but is about 45% built; first tests about Oct 2026; EU evaluation of the yellow card pushed to 2027 (La Estrella). Only 70 of 481 longliners have VMS (DE 126/2017). ARAP-OIRSA agreement Feb 2026. ARAP has a ROP form for artisanal fishing organisations. EUDR roadmap for coffee, cocoa, beef, palm, timber started Oct 2025. AUPSA/APA import side covered by K09 (rejected).

coverage.category: 31. Gaming: casinos, type A gaming rooms, slot-machine operators (Junta de Control de Juegos)
coverage.found: Ley 527 (Gaceta Oficial 28 May 2026): casinos and type A rooms must integrate facial recognition into CCTV to spot people excluded by the JCJ; online operators need biometric age checks and spending limits; operators pay 0.5% of payouts to the Treasury; JCJ audits yearly; fines $25k-$100k; ISP blocking orders up to $1m. JCJ and AIG are building a map of venues and machine IDs; no operator filing described. Compliance dates not stated. Candidate listed as weak.

coverage.category: 32. Fisheries: artisanal fishing organisations, vessel owners, processing plants
coverage.found: See category 30. State system is still being built, so a private product cannot plug in yet. Candidate listed as unverified.

coverage.category: 33. Colon Free Zone users and adjacent-area operators
coverage.found: Junta Directiva resolution JD 001-2026 (12 Feb 2026, Gaceta 24 Mar 2026): adjacent-area operators must notify changes, file sub-tenant documents, keep to authorised activities, allow inspections, add perimeter security and record operations in the Declaracion de Movimiento Comercial. Existing operators get up to 12 months to adjust (about Mar 2027). No periodic report for ordinary ZLC users found. Candidate listed as unverified.

coverage.category: 34. Waste and oily-waste generators (workshops, lubricentros, tyre dealers)
coverage.found: Ley 6/2007 covers generators, carriers and recyclers of oily waste and uses a registration document that tracks transport and destination. Ley 518 (Apr 2026) is about tyres in asphalt. No extended-producer-responsibility regime or importer register found. Candidate listed as unverified.

coverage.category: 35. Medicinal cannabis licensees and sellers (Ley 242/2021, DE 6/2025)
coverage.found: DNFD Comunicado 019-DNFD-2026: licence modification for increase of activity before selling; extra authorisation from the licence holder; notarised document for pharmacies already handling controlled products, technical inspection for others. A one-off step for few firms. Weak.

coverage.category: 36. Beneficial-owner declarations in public procurement and SSNF registers
coverage.found: DE 40/2018 requires beneficial-owner declarations for legal entities and consortia bidding for public contracts; SSNF backed a rule on this (La Estrella). Falls on firms already served by resident agents (K01). Nothing new.

Registro Nacional de Buhoneros (MICI) plus a municipal permit with sworn declaration, area sketch, cedula and health cards. Reglamento due within 6 months.

coverage.category: 19. Market traders, street vendors, money changers
coverage.found: Street vendors: new Ley 540 of 2 Jul 2026 (Gaceta Oficial 30560, 3 Jul 2026) creates a Registro Nacional de Buhoneros (MICI, with municipal registers) and a municipal 'permiso de acreditación de buhonero autorizado'. It covers fixed, semi-fixed, ambulant and seasonal stalls. Requirements: Panamanian citizen, cedula copy, registry entry, sworn declaration of the activity, sketch of the area, and valid blanco/verde health cards for food sellers. Applies 3 months after promulgation (about Oct 2026; exact date unconfirmed). Existing unauthorised vendors get 120 calendar days to apply, so a deadline falls around Feb 2027. The Executive has up to 6 months to issue the reglamento (about Jan 2027). Fees, renewal term and penalties are not in the sources. Vendors are individual informal sellers with little ability to pay. The Municipio de Panamá already runs its own 'Sistema de Microempresarios y Buhoneros' (permits, space allocation, QR validation, 95% complete, started 13 Oct 2025) per its open-data inventory. Seasonal permits (fiestas patrias, Christmas, Carnaval via ATP draw) are handled by the alcaldía, MINSA, Bomberos and Aseo, around B/.80 in total. Municipal market stalls (Acuerdo 50/2025 amending Acuerdo 132/2020) require health cards, an MICI aviso de operación and a sworn declaration; the tenant rent data found is old, with no collection system confirmed. Lottery sellers (billeteros): about 13,000 per the LNB director, who holds a 'libreta' under Decreto de Gabinete 224/1969, with audits of guarantees and social-work reports and about 200 libretas suspended. Money changers: these are SBP-supervised financial obliged subjects (Ley 23/2015 as amended by Ley 21/2017; Acuerdo 002-2018 registration; quarterly remittance reports; audited financials by 15 April; SBP resolution RG-PSO-2025-00671 of Oct 2025 updates information requirements for 'other financial obliged subjects'). The assignment note puts this outside the niche, so no deeper work was done.

result.competitor: Three searches in Spanish ("software cumplimiento Ley 23 sujetos no financieros", "software prevención blanqueo SSNF joyerías empeño", "casas de empeño joyerías software SSNF") found no software or app built for Panamanian pawnshops or jewellers, and no free SSNF portal that runs PEP screening or the risk matrix. The SSNF publishes free materials: a client risk-matrix guide and a pawnshop sector-risk document. The UAF runs an online filing platform for reports. I did not search by name for generic AML/PEP-screening vendors or local compliance consultancies, so their presence and prices are not_reached. They very likely exist and are the real substitute.
result.duty: The duty is real and in force in Panama. Ley 23/2015 lists pawnshops (casas de empeño) and traders in precious metals and stones as non-financial obligated subjects (Deloitte, KPMG). Ley 124/2020 created the SSNF as their supervisor, and DE 35/2022 regulates the law (PwC). The duties are: register with SSNF/UAF (Res. S-010-2021), keep a client risk matrix (SSNF guide 2022), do due diligence and identify beneficial owners at 25%, and file cash and near-cash transaction reports for amounts of B/.10,000 or more, including split payments, plus suspicious-activity reports to the UAF. Res. S-022-2025 (21 Mar 2025, Gaceta 30248) adds self-assessment risk questionnaires for non-financial obligated subjects. I could not open the full text (the PDF was too large), so the frequency and deadline are unverified. Res. S-008-2026 (Gaceta 30487-B, 20 Mar 2026, in force on publication) requires enhanced due diligence on PEPs with standardised forms, checks in open sources, ongoing monitoring and a 2-year tail after leaving office. La Estrella names jewellers explicitly; pawnshops are not named but are covered as non-financial obligated subjects. Penalties: the claim's $1M is not verified. PwC reports a reform that raised AML penalties up to $5M.
result.market: Pawnshops: 190 authorised according to MICI (date unclear) and about 255 in November 2018 (Panamá América). I found no figure for registered jewellers or precious-metal traders, and no SSNF count of obligated subjects by sector. Whether "compro oro" buyers are registered is unverified. Estimated total: a few hundred businesses, possibly 300-600, which is small.
result.reason: The duty is real and recent: PEP enhanced due diligence (S-008-2026), self-assessment questionnaires (S-022-2025), a risk matrix, and UAF cash and suspicious reports, all under an active supervisor that ran 3,064 on-site inspections in 2022. I found no sector-specific product. However, the market is tiny (about 190-255 pawnshops plus an unknown number of jewellers). Pawnshops are reportedly under financial strain, so willingness to pay is likely low. Generic AML screening tools and consultancies probably cover the core job. Distribution through the pawnbrokers' association (Asociación de Entidades Prendarias) is plausible. An MVP of forms, a risk matrix and a cash-transaction log is simple. Still, the small market caps revenue unless the product also covers other non-financial obligated subjects (K03 real estate, used cars).

result.competitor: I found no Panama-specific software that produces the DNFD controlled-substances book or quarterly report. Results were generic Spanish, US and LatAm pharmacy point-of-sale (POS) and ERP tools: softwaredoit.es, LOC Software, and an Odoo integrator (ecosire) with a generic controlled-substance tracking feature. DNFD's own FADDI portal handles licences and permits, not this report, as far as I found. I could not check local POS vendors or the in-house systems of pharmacy chains.
result.duty: Real and current as of the last notice found. Comunicado 021-2024/DNFD (14 March 2024) requires every licensed pharmacy to send a quarterly controlled-substances report from Q1 2024 on. It is one colour-scanned PDF of the official paper form, e-mailed to monitoreoanalisis@minsa.gob.pa with the licence number and quarter in the subject line. It must include purchases and returns; pharmacies without controlled stock send only the cover page. Legal base: Ley 419 of 1 February 2024 (replaces Ley 1/2001) and its regulation, Decreto Ejecutivo 27 of 10 May 2024 (Gaceta 30028-C). A 2016 Gaceta resolution gives DNFD the job of verifying establishments' controlled-substance records and compiling the quarterly reports it sends to the INCB (the UN drug-control board). Penalty: not found; I could not locate the sanctions article. I found no 2025-2026 notice replacing the e-mail process, but no source confirms it is unchanged either. The DNFD PDFs could not be parsed, so the details come from search excerpts and the inspection share was not re-checked.
result.market: Not reached: I found no current count of licensed pharmacies. Salud y Farmacos (2025) says 110 pharmacies take part in the low-cost medicines programme, which is a lower bound only. The MINSA list of laboratories and droguerias is from 2019-2020. The total is plausibly in the hundreds to low thousands, but that is unverified.
result.reason: Search excerpts of DNFD Comunicado 021-2024 (14 March 2024) say that from Q1 2024 every pharmacy e-mails a quarterly controlled-substances report as a PDF to monitoreoanalisis@minsa.gob.pa. Pharmacies with no controlled stock still send the cover page. Ley 419/2024 and its rules, DE 27/2024, are in force. I found no newer notice and no Panama-specific product that fills or generates this report. FADDI covers licences, not this report (per the 2024 notices). Weak points: I could not find the sanctions or the pharmacy count, and I could not rule out local point-of-sale (POS) systems. The job is a small scan-and-send task four times a year, so willingness to pay is low and the product is a feature rather than a business. DNFD could also move the report onto FADDI.

The duty is real but weak and unstable. VMS is required for longliners under DE 126/2017, but DE 13/2023 limited it to mid and large vessels, and ARAP admits enforcement gaps. Logbooks are reportedly not even requested. ARAP is building the national traceability system itself (about 45% done, tests around Oct 2026, EU review in Q1 2027), funded by a $7.2M credit and run with OIRSA. ITRA and Elan are already validated for transshipments and landings. MarViva is working on artisanal traceability in the Gulf of Chiriquí. I did not fetch ARAP's Formato-ROP and found no register count beyond 481 longliners. Buyers are few and poor and the rules are in flux. The scope is mostly state-system integration, not a recurring private filing, so I could not confirm it.

The EUDR duty falls on EU operators and traders, not on Panamanian exporters or co-ops. I found no Panamanian rule that binds exporters. Dates have moved: 30 Dec 2026 for medium and large operators, 30 Jun 2027 for micro and small ones. The claim's dates are outdated. Free tools already do the core job. Fairtrade Plot Insights (June 2026) is free to certified co-ops, runs risk analysis through Satelligence, and shares data from October via Fairtrace. CLAC supports more than 800 Latin American co-ops with it. TechnoServe's TerraTrac is a free geolocation app. Panama's coffee and cocoa export base is tiny, and I found no count. The MIDA/Panama search returned no EUDR programme.

Duty is real. Ley 23/2015 makes savings-and-credit and multi-service co-ops obliged subjects, with IPACOOP as AML supervisor on a risk basis. Press says 175 of 583 co-ops are in scope. In Aug 2025 IPACOOP cancelled SUNTRACS R.L.'s legal status. The reported findings included no risk matrix, no customer risk tiers, no monitoring system and incomplete KYC files. That shows enforcement and the shape of the product. Weaknesses: the buyer pool is small (about 175), and many are not tiny. I found no Panama-specific AML tool for co-ops, but I did not search vendors in depth, and core-banking vendors likely bundle AML modules. Penalty amounts, filing frequency and the current IPACOOP/UAF rules were not checked. Sources are mostly 2014-2015 articles plus one 2025 news item.
